channel.title: Bella — the treatment coordinator blog
channel.description: Practical writing on case acceptance, treatment presentation, and the treatment coordinator role.

item.title: What to say when a parent says “I need to think about it”
item.description: It is rarely about thinking. Four things that sentence usually means, and how to find out which one you are hearing.

item.title: When to stop selling and get the doctor
item.description: Some objections are financial. Some are clinical. Continuing to work a clinical objection as a coordinator is the fastest way to lose a family for good.

item.title: Treatment coordinator bonus structures that don’t distort behavior
item.description: Pay a coordinator on case acceptance and you will get case acceptance — including the cases that should not have been accepted. How to design a bonus that does not backfire.

item.title: What to look for when hiring a treatment coordinator
item.description: Most practices hire for dental experience and end up disappointed. The traits that actually predict a good coordinator, and how to test for them in an interview.

item.title: Presenting pediatric treatment when the child isn’t in pain
item.description: The hardest case in pediatric dentistry: a parent looking at a happy, comfortable child and being told they need to spend two thousand dollars.

item.title: Stop handing over the printout
item.description: The treatment plan printout is a summary of a conversation, not a substitute for one. What happens when you lead with paper — and what to do instead.

item.title: Build the value before you say the price. Actually do it.
item.description: Everyone agrees with this in principle and almost nobody does it in the room. What building value looks like in a real treatment presentation.

item.title: The silence after you say the number
item.description: Most coordinators lose the case in the four seconds after they state the price. Why the pause feels unbearable, and what happens when you let it sit.

item.title: How to explain PPO and HMO without using the words PPO or HMO
item.description: Parents do not care what their plan is called. They care what it pays. A plain-language way through the insurance conversation that avoids the usual traps.

item.title: “Can we just do the one tooth?”
item.description: Phasing treatment is legitimate. Cherry-picking is not. How to tell which one a parent is asking for, and what to say when the answer is no.

item.title: “Let me check with my husband”
item.description: Usually true, usually fatal. The case does not die in your office — it dies at a kitchen table you are not sitting at. Here is how to survive that conversation.
